sections.title: Two locations can change at the same time
paragraphs: A developing follicle is in an ovary. The endometrium is the lining of the uterus. A cycle description becomes confusing if those two locations are treated as one structure with one set of events. We will follow the ovarian structures and uterine lining together, then explain the hormonal connection between them.

The ovarian cycle includes follicle development, ovulation and corpus-luteum activity. A follicle contains an oocyte and supporting cells. Ovulation releases the secondary oocyte; remaining follicular tissue can form the corpus luteum. The uterine cycle describes changes in the endometrium, including shedding, rebuilding and maintenance of the lining.

Hormones provide a link between the organs. Developing follicles release estrogen, which helps the endometrium grow. After ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone and some estrogen, supporting the prepared lining. The hormones travel in blood; the follicle and corpus luteum remain in the ovary.

In the illustrative 28-day model used here, day 1 is the first day of menstrual flow and ovulation is placed near day 14. These numbers help align the drawings. They are not a timetable for every person or a way to identify guaranteed pregnancy-free days. A stated biological event is stronger evidence for a phase boundary than an assumed calendar number.

sections.title: Menstrual flow overlaps early follicular activity
paragraphs: The follicular phase is the ovarian phase before ovulation. The luteal phase is the ovarian phase after ovulation, when the corpus luteum is active. Menstruation, or menstrual flow, is the shedding of part of the uterine lining. It names a uterine event, not a third ovarian phase that must finish before follicles can develop.

Near the end of a cycle without pregnancy support, the corpus luteum regresses and its progesterone and estrogen output falls. The endometrium loses hormonal support and part of it is shed. The first day of that flow is counted as day 1 of the next cycle.

As the previous cycle's ovarian-hormone restraint declines, follicle-stimulating hormone, FSH, can support development of follicles in the ovary. This activity can already be underway when flow begins. Thus a uterus shedding lining and an ovary developing follicles are compatible observations, not evidence that one of the observations must be wrong.

As follicular estrogen output rises, it helps rebuild the endometrium. The new follicle does not cause the preceding hormone withdrawal merely because its development overlaps flow. Keep the sequence of causes separate from the fact that two events occur at the same time.

The teacher slides list flow and a later follicular interval as successive teaching landmarks. For ovarian phase names, however, include the early flow days within the follicular phase. This preserves the distinction between which organ is being described and when the event occurs.

sections.title: Ovulation changes the main ovarian structure
paragraphs: Ovulation marks the transition from the ovarian follicular phase to the luteal phase. It is the release event, not the number 14 itself, that defines the boundary. If a stated model places ovulation later, the phase boundary moves with that event.

After release, the follicular tissue left in the ovary becomes the corpus luteum. Its progesterone, together with estrogen, helps maintain and prepare the endometrium for possible implantation. An early embryo would implant in this lining later; ovulation itself is neither fertilization nor implantation.

Read the retained diagram in rows first. The top row follows ovarian events from early follicular development, through later development, to an active corpus luteum after ovulation. The bottom row follows uterine flow, rebuilding and maintenance. Then compare the paired boxes in each column to see events that overlap in time.

The vertical arrows connect the ovarian and uterine rows for comparison. In the first column, read the link as overlap: developing follicles do not directly cause menstrual flow. Flow follows the preceding fall in ovarian-hormone support, as the note below the diagram states. In the later columns, estrogen and progesterone explain the hormonal links to growth and maintenance. The boxes are not drawn to give exact durations.

The diagram therefore supports two kinds of reading: left-to-right sequence within one organ, and simultaneous or hormonally connected events across organs. Neither arrow direction means that a follicle, oocyte or corpus luteum travels down into the uterine lining.

sections.title: The end of one cycle helps explain the start of the next
paragraphs: If pregnancy is not established, corpus-luteum activity declines. Progesterone and estrogen fall, the lining is no longer maintained in the same way, and menstrual flow follows. This hormone sequence connects the later luteal phase with the next cycle's day 1.

An unfertilized oocyte has a limited viable life after ovulation. Its loss does not instantly stop corpus-luteum hormone production. The retained tissue can remain active for days afterwards, which is why an explanation of flow timing must follow the hormone-producing tissue rather than the egg alone.

A hormonal connection also requires a responsive target. An ovarian source can release a hormone into blood while a uterine tissue fails to make its usual response. To explain a new observation, identify the source, the signal, the target and the target's normal job before deciding which part of the relationship has changed.

The core sequence is now connected: follicular estrogen helps rebuild the lining, luteal hormones support it after ovulation, and their later decline permits shedding. We will next read the changing pituitary and ovarian hormone patterns that coordinate this sequence.

worked.title: A normal signal with a changed uterine response
worked.scenario: In a stated model after ovulation, the corpus luteum releases progesterone normally, but the endometrium cannot make its usual response to that hormone. Does normal ovarian output alone establish normal maintenance of the lining?
steps: Identify the source and signal: the corpus luteum is in the ovary and releases progesterone into blood. The model keeps that output normal.
Identify the target: the endometrium in the uterus. Its usual response to progesterone helps maintain and prepare the lining after ovulation.
Apply the changed condition. A signal's presence does not supply the missing target response. Normal progesterone output alone therefore cannot establish normal progesterone-dependent maintenance.

Check the conclusion's limits. The model does not say that ovulation failed, the corpus luteum moved into the uterus or all other hormone responses stopped. It also does not give enough information to predict an exact day of bleeding. The specific failed link is signal-to-target response.

optional.question: A hypothetical cycle record states that ovulation occurred on day 18. On day 16 a follicle was still developing and estrogen was rising. Which ovarian phase fits day 16, and what uterine change would estrogen normally support? Explain why simply calling every day after 14 luteal would misread this record.
optional.answer: Day 16 is still follicular because it precedes the stated ovulation event on day 18. Rising follicular estrogen normally supports endometrial growth. The ovarian luteal phase begins after ovulation, so transferring day 14 mechanically from a different illustrative model would assign the boundary to the wrong event.

sections.title: Name the hormone source before interpreting a curve
paragraphs: A hormone curve records how a quantity changes over time; it does not show the producing gland directly. Before following its peaks, connect each hormone with its source and job. GnRH, gonadotropin-releasing hormone, comes from the hypothalamus and stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH.

FSH, follicle-stimulating hormone, supports follicular development in the ovary. LH, luteinizing hormone, contributes to ovarian activity and its surge helps trigger ovulation. These are pituitary signals arriving at ovarian tissue. Estrogen and progesterone in this cycle are outputs of ovarian tissue rather than hormones made by the anterior pituitary.

As the dominant follicle develops, its estrogen output increases. Estrogen supports endometrial growth. Through much of the follicular phase, estrogen also contributes to negative feedback that limits further pituitary stimulation, especially FSH. Negative feedback is a response that tends to oppose the original change; it does not mean the hormone is harmful.

Keep direct and later effects separate. FSH supports a developing follicle, the follicle produces estrogen, and estrogen affects the uterine lining. Calling all of these 'female hormones' would hide the source-to-target links that explain a graph.

sections.title: Sustained high estrogen precedes the LH surge
paragraphs: Near the end of follicular development, sufficiently high estrogen sustained over time changes the feedback response. Instead of restraining the control system, this ovarian signal promotes a strong pituitary LH surge: a large, brief rise in LH release. Positive feedback means that a response reinforces or amplifies activity in the pathway.

The LH surge helps trigger release of the secondary oocyte and the changes that form the corpus luteum from remaining follicular tissue. FSH also has a smaller rise around this event. The large, narrow LH peak is therefore a useful landmark when reading the normal model, but it is a hormone event linked to ovulation, not a picture of the oocyte itself.

The positive-feedback interval is temporary and depends on the stage and sustained signal. It does not mean every estrogen increase always raises LH, that all inhibition disappears permanently, or that hormone levels become fixed after the surge. 'Estrogen inhibits the pituitary' and 'estrogen helps produce an LH surge' describe different conditions in the same cycle.

To explain the switch, state both conditions and direction: ordinary follicular feedback helps restrain stimulation, whereas sustained high pre-ovulatory estrogen promotes the surge. A single measurement without its timing and pattern does not establish which response is occurring.

sections.title: Follow the post-ovulatory ovarian output
paragraphs: After ovulation, an active corpus luteum releases progesterone and some estrogen. Progesterone rises and supports the endometrium. The luteal hormones also contribute to negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary system, helping limit the stimulation that would support another ovulatory event during this phase.

Without pregnancy support, the corpus luteum regresses. Its progesterone and estrogen output falls, reducing support for the lining and contributing to the next menstrual flow. A broad progesterone rise after ovulation fits the change from follicle to corpus luteum; it should not be placed as the cause of the earlier follicle's initial growth.

Estrogen can show a smaller rise during the luteal phase as well as the larger pre-ovulatory rise. Read the whole pattern rather than insisting that a hormone must come from only one ovarian structure or have only one peak. These sketches simplify a continuous process and do not show every regulating hormone.

sections.title: Read timing and scale from the actual graph
paragraphs: Begin with the axes. Both panels in the retained figure use cycle day horizontally, with day 1 marking the start of menstrual flow in this illustration. The vertical axes say relative level. There are no measured blood-concentration units or numerical vertical ticks. Each curve is separately scaled, so a line twice as high is not evidence of twice the hormone concentration.

Read the key with line pattern as well as colour. In the upper panel, solid reddish LH has the narrow high peak near day 14; dashed brown FSH has a smaller rise near that event and a modest earlier rise. In the lower panel, solid teal estrogen rises before the large LH peak and has a smaller later rise. Dashed dark-green progesterone rises later, with a broad maximum near the third week of the illustrated cycle.

Compare the curves against the same day marks: the estrogen rise precedes the LH surge, and the broad progesterone rise follows it. Then connect each to biology: developing follicle, pituitary surge/ovulation, active corpus luteum. The line segment close to the bottom is a low relative level in this schematic; it does not prove that a hormone is completely absent.

Curve height, concentration and rate of change are different comparisons. Timing of peaks can be compared here because the panels share the day axis. Change within one curve can be described qualitatively as rising or falling. Absolute concentration ratios and numerical rates cannot be calculated from this figure because the vertical scale supplies no measured values.

For a new graph, inspect its own units, vertical ranges, labels and stated conditions. A different colour is not a different hormone, and a shifted peak should not be forced onto day 14. Identify the observed change, connect it to the model, and state what the record does not establish. These teaching graphs are not individual observations or a personal fertility calendar.

An observation record also has a sampling limit. A brief peak might fall between measurements or outside the recorded interval. A missing recorded peak therefore does not by itself establish that the biological event never happened; first distinguish what was measured from what remains unobserved.

worked.title: A taller trace can represent a smaller measured value
worked.scenario: Consider a constructed scale-reading exercise, not patient data. Graph A has a vertical range from 0 to 20 units/L; its marked point is three-quarters of the way up. Graph B has the same displayed height but a vertical range from 0 to 200 units/L; its point is halfway up. Both use linear vertical scales and the same stated unit. Which point has the larger numerical value?
steps: Read the range before comparing height. Graph A's full height represents 20 units/L, while Graph B's full height represents 200 units/L. Equal centimetres on the page do not represent equal amounts.

Convert each position using its own axis. Three-quarters of 20 is 15 units/L. Half of 200 is 100 units/L. The linear scales begin at zero in this exercise, so these fractions apply directly to the full ranges.
Compare the values in their common unit: 100 units/L is greater than 15 units/L, even though Graph B's point is drawn lower. The naive height comparison gives the wrong conclusion.

Return to the retained cycle schematic. It does not provide these numerical ranges at all, so we cannot perform the same conversion or calculate concentration ratios from it. We can still compare the timing of rises and peaks along its day axis.
Keep the example bounded. The invented numbers demonstrate axis reading; they are not normal ranges for LH, FSH, estrogen or progesterone, and do not support a diagnosis.

optional.question: A hypothetical record meets the model's sustained-high-estrogen condition but shows no recorded LH surge in the following observation interval. Which expected relationship is missing from that record? Explain why this alone does not prove a particular cause or establish that ovulation never occurred.
optional.answer: The normal-model sequence links sustained high pre-ovulatory estrogen with a later LH surge. The record lacks a recorded surge in the stated interval, so that expected link is not demonstrated. The observation interval and sampling may not capture every event, and the record does not identify why the pattern differs. It supports a bounded description of the missing observed event, not a diagnosis or a claim about every time outside the record.
